questions.text: An Ellingham diagram plots, against temperature, the standard free-energy change for:

options.label: a
options.text: The formation of a compound (usually an oxide) from the elements, expressed per mole of $O_2$ consumed

questions.detailed: An Ellingham diagram is a graph of $\Delta G^\circ$ versus $T$ for reactions such as $\frac{2x}{y}M+O_2=\frac{2}{y}M_xO_y$, written per mole of $O_2$. It is the master chart for deciding which metal can reduce which oxide.

questions.text: On an Ellingham diagram, the slope of each line equals:
questions.detailed: Since $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$, plotting against $T$ gives a line of slope $-\Delta S^\circ$ and intercept $\Delta H^\circ$. This is why the shape of each line is controlled by its entropy of reaction.

questions.text: Most metal-oxidation lines on an Ellingham diagram slope *upward* because:

options.label: a
options.text: The reaction consumes gaseous $O_2$, so $\Delta S^\circ<0$ and the slope $-\Delta S^\circ>0$

questions.detailed: Oxidation removes a mole of $O_2$ gas (high entropy) and forms a condensed oxide (low entropy), so $\Delta S^\circ<0$. Hence the slope $-\Delta S^\circ$ is positive and lines climb with temperature: oxides become less stable as $T$ rises.

questions.text: Why does an Ellingham line show a kink at the melting point of the metal?

options.label: a
options.text: The entropy of the metal jumps at the phase change, changing the slope

questions.detailed: At a phase transition the entropy of the species changes sharply (latent heat / $T$), so $\Delta S^\circ$ of the overall reaction changes and the line's slope ($-\Delta S^\circ$) changes — a kink. A larger kink occurs at the boiling point.

questions.text: On an Ellingham diagram, the more stable an oxide is, the:

options.label: a
options.text: Lower its line lies on the diagram

questions.detailed: A more negative $\Delta G^\circ_f$ means a lower position on the plot (more negative). So a metal whose oxide line lies *below* another's can reduce that other oxide.

questions.text: Metal M can reduce the oxide of metal N if, at the temperature of interest:

options.label: a
options.text: M's oxide line lies *below* N's oxide line, giving a combined $\Delta G^\circ<0$

options.label: b
options.text: M's oxide line lies above N's oxide line

questions.detailed: Combine the two reactions: oxidise M (reverse of M's oxide formation) and reduce N's oxide. The net $\Delta G^\circ$ is favourable (<0) when M's oxide is more stable — i.e. its line lies below N's. This is the basis of metallothermic reduction (e.g. Al reducing FeO).

questions.text: On the Ellingham diagram, the point O at the top left (T = 0, $\Delta G^\circ=0$) is important because:

options.label: a
options.text: All constant-$p_{O_2}$ lines pass through it, enabling the oxygen nomographic scale

options.label: b
options.text: It marks the melting point of iron

options.label: c
options.text: It is the triple point of water

questions.detailed: At equilibrium $\Delta G^\circ=RT\ln p_{O_2}$, which vanishes as $T\to0$ regardless of $p_{O_2}$. Hence every isobar for $p_{O_2}$ emanates from the common origin O, the basis of the nomographic oxygen scale on real Ellingham diagrams.

questions.text: The carbon oxidation lines on an Ellingham diagram are unusual because:

options.label: a
options.text: $C+O_2\to CO_2$ is nearly horizontal, while $2C+O_2\to 2CO$ has a strong negative slope (gas is produced)

questions.detailed: $C+O_2=CO_2$ consumes one gas and makes one gas, so $\Delta S^\circ\approx0$ — nearly horizontal. $2C+O_2=2CO$ turns one gas into two, $\Delta S^\circ>0$, so its slope is strongly negative. The descending CO line crosses many metal-oxide lines at high $T$, making carbon a powerful high-temperature reductant.

questions.text: A reaction has $\Delta G^\circ=100{,}000-100\,T\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. Above what temperature does it become thermodynamically favourable?
questions.detailed: Set $\Delta G^\circ=0$: $100{,}000-100T=0\Rightarrow T=1000\ \mathrm{K}$. Above 1000 K the entropic term dominates and $\Delta G^\circ<0$; the slope here is $-\Delta S^\circ=-100\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

questions.text: The Boudouard reaction, important in the blast furnace, is:
questions.detailed: The Boudouard reaction is $C+CO_2\rightleftharpoons 2CO$. It is endothermic and strongly entropy-favoured (1 gas → 2 gas), so it becomes favourable at high temperature — the key to producing CO, the actual reducing gas in ironmaking.

questions.text: At equilibrium between a metal, its oxide and oxygen gas, the relation between $\Delta G^\circ$ and the oxygen partial pressure is:
questions.detailed: For $\frac{2x}{y}M+O_2=\frac{2}{y}M_xO_y$ at equilibrium, $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln p_{O_2}$. A very negative $\Delta G^\circ$ corresponds to an extremely low equilibrium oxygen pressure — a very stable oxide.

questions.text: For the reaction $2C+O_2=2CO$, $\Delta H^\circ=-221\ \mathrm{kJ}$ and $\Delta S^\circ=+179\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The slope of its Ellingham line is:
questions.detailed: Slope $=-\Delta S^\circ=-179\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, so the line slopes *downward* with increasing $T$. Combined with a negative intercept, this makes the CO line plunge below many oxide lines at high temperature.

questions.text: Which statement about the use of the oxygen scale on an Ellingham diagram is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: Joining the origin O to a point on an oxide line at temperature $T$ and extending to the $p_{O_2}$ axis gives the equilibrium oxygen pressure

options.label: b
options.text: The oxygen scale is read directly off the $y$-axis

options.label: c
options.text: The oxygen scale applies only at 298 K

options.label: d
options.text: There is no oxygen scale on Ellingham diagrams

questions.detailed: Because all $p_{O_2}$ isobars pass through O, the equilibrium oxygen pressure at any point is found by drawing a line from O through that point to the calibrated $p_{O_2}$ scale on the right — a quick graphical way to read reducing conditions.

questions.text: In practice, CO is a better reductant for FeO than solid carbon directly because:

options.label: a
options.text: CO is a gas and reacts with the oxide at the surface, while carbon first forms CO via the Boudouard reaction

options.label: c
options.text: CO has a lower affinity for oxygen

questions.detailed: Solid carbon cannot contact the oxide intimately, so it is gasified by $CO_2$ (Boudouard) to $CO$, which then reduces FeO: $FeO+CO\rightleftharpoons Fe+CO_2$. The net effect is indirect reduction; the CO/CO\_2 ratio governs it.

questions.text: For $FeO+CO=Fe+CO_2$, at equilibrium the ratio $p_{CO}/p_{CO_2}$ is fixed by temperature. If the equilibrium constant at 1000 K is 0.5, the required $p_{CO}/p_{CO_2}$ to reduce FeO is:
questions.detailed: $K=p_{CO_2}/p_{CO}=0.5$, so the equilibrium ratio is $p_{CO}/p_{CO_2}=1/K=2$. To reduce FeO the gas must be more reducing than equilibrium, i.e. $p_{CO}/p_{CO_2}>2$; hence 2.0 is the threshold value. The reducing power of CO is set by the CO/CO2 ratio versus temperature.

questions.text: Ellingham diagrams exist not only for oxides but also, in analogous form, for:

options.label: a
options.text: Sulfides, chlorides and nitrides (formation of compounds from the elements)

questions.detailed: The same construction applies to sulfides, chlorides, carbides and nitrides. The relative positions of the lines tell you, for example, whether a metal can reduce a sulfide or whether a chloride can be reduced by another metal.

questions.text: The approximately straight lines on an Ellingham diagram rely on the assumption that, over the range plotted:

options.label: a
options.text: $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are nearly constant with temperature

questions.detailed: If $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ vary only weakly with $T$, then $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$ is essentially linear in $T$. The slight curvature and the kinks come from heat-capacity and phase changes.

questions.text: The standard free energy of formation of $Al_2O_3$ is far more negative than that of $FeO$ at all temperatures. This means aluminium:

options.label: a
options.text: Can reduce FeO, releasing much heat — the basis of the aluminothermic (thermite) reaction

questions.detailed: The $Al_2O_3$ line lies well below the FeO line, so $3FeO+2Al\to Al_2O_3+3Fe$ has a large negative $\Delta G^\circ$ — exploited in the highly exothermic thermite reaction.

questions.text: Which statements about reading an Ellingham diagram are correct?

statements.text: A lower line means a more stable oxide.
A metal can reduce the oxide of a metal whose line lies above it at that temperature.
The slope of a line gives the entropy of the formation reaction.

questions.detailed: All three are correct. Lower line = more stable oxide (I); a metal below can reduce an oxide above it (II); and the slope is $-\Delta S^\circ$, so it carries the entropy information (III).

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: A metal whose oxide forms with a very large negative $\Delta G^\circ$ is a strong reducing agent.
questions.reason: Such a metal has a high affinity for oxygen, so it can strip oxygen from the oxides of less reactive metals.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: A very negative $\Delta G^\circ_f$ of its oxide means the metal binds oxygen strongly (high affinity), so it readily reduces less stable oxides. R is exactly the physical reason for A. Magnesium and aluminium are classic examples.

questions.text: For $2Mg+O_2=2MgO$, $\Delta G^\circ=-1{,}200{,}000+400\,T\ \mathrm{J}$. Above approximately what temperature does MgO cease to be stable (in isolation)?
questions.detailed: Set $\Delta G^\circ=0$: $T=1{,}200{,}000/400=3000\ \mathrm{K}$. Below 3000 K MgO is stable ($\Delta G^\circ<0$); this high value reflects the exceptional stability of MgO, which is why Mg is such a strong reductant.

questions.text: The main reason a metal oxide can be reduced by carbon at high temperature is:

options.label: a
options.text: The $2C+O_2\to2CO$ line descends with temperature and eventually crosses below the oxide line

questions.detailed: Because $2C+O_2=2CO$ has a negative slope (entropy-driven), its line eventually lies below metal-oxide lines as $T$ rises. At that crossing temperature, $M_xO_y+...C\to M+CO$ becomes thermodynamically favourable — the basis of carbothermic reduction.

questions.text: Below the line of an oxide $\frac{2x}{y}M+O_2=\frac{2}{y}M_xO_y$, the stable phase is:

options.label: c
options.text: A mixture of M and O

questions.detailed: The line itself corresponds to $\Delta G^\circ=0$ (equilibrium). Below the line $\Delta G^\circ<0$, so the oxide is the stable product; above the line the metal is stable. Real diagrams mark the fields for metal and oxide on either side.

questions.text: A free-energy function calculation gives for the formation of a particular oxide $\Delta G^\circ=-500{,}000+150\,T\ \mathrm{J}$. At $1000\ \mathrm{K}$, $\Delta G^\circ$ is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta G^\circ=-500{,}000+150(1000)=-500{,}000+150{,}000=-350{,}000\ \mathrm{J}$. Still strongly negative at 1000 K, so the oxide remains stable there.

questions.text: The "couple" $2C+O_2=2CO$ and $2CO+O_2=2CO_2$ is useful because together they:

options.label: a
options.text: Define the CO/CO$_2$ ratio that controls whether a metal oxide is reduced by carbon

options.label: d
options.text: Give the melting point of carbon

questions.detailed: Subtracting the two carbon lines gives the equilibrium $2CO\rightleftharpoons C+CO_2$ (Boudouard), which fixes the $p_{CO}/p_{CO_2}$ ratio at any temperature. Whether a given oxide is reduced depends on whether the gas composition lies on the reducing side of the oxide's own $p_{CO}/p_{CO_2}$ equilibrium.

questions.text: "A metal whose oxide line lies above another metal's oxide line can be used to reduce that other oxide."
questions.detailed: False. The reducing metal's oxide line must lie *below* the oxide being reduced, so the combined $\Delta G^\circ<0$. A metal whose oxide is less stable (line above) cannot strip oxygen from a more stable oxide.

questions.text: Match the feature of an Ellingham diagram (List I) with its meaning (List II):
questions.detailed: Slope = $-\Delta S^\circ$ (P-1); $T=0$ intercept = $\Delta H^\circ$ (Q-2); kink = phase transition (R-3); point O = origin for all $p_{O_2}$ lines (S-4). Together these let you read enthalpy, entropy and equilibrium oxygen pressure from the chart.

questions.text: Which of the following is *not* directly obtainable from an Ellingham diagram?

options.label: b
options.text: The temperature at which two reactions balance

questions.detailed: Ellingham diagrams are purely thermodynamic — they say whether a reaction is favourable, not how fast it goes. A reduction may be thermodynamically allowed yet kinetically slow, needing a catalyst or higher temperature for acceptable rate.
